title: Kubernetes Networking
subtitle: Pod networking, Services, Ingress and NetworkPolicies
description: Understand how traffic flows in a cluster: the Pod network and DNS, Services, Ingress routing with TLS, and NetworkPolicies to lock it down.
outcomes: Explain the Kubernetes network model and cluster DNS
Expose workloads with Services and Ingress
Restrict and debug traffic with NetworkPolicies

modules.title: Pod networking and Services
modules.summary: The network model, DNS and Service types.

lessons.title: The network model and cluster DNS
lessons.summary: Every Pod gets its own IP, Pods reach each other without NAT, and CoreDNS turns Service names into addresses.
objectives: State the four rules of the Kubernetes network model
Explain the role of the CNI plugin
Resolve Services and Pods through cluster DNS names

sections.title: Flat, NAT-free Pod networking
sections.body:
Kubernetes imposes a simple model: every **Pod gets its own IP address**, every Pod can reach every other Pod **without NAT**, and agents on a node (such as the kubelet) can reach all Pods on that node. Containers in the same Pod share one network namespace, so they talk over `localhost` and must not bind the same port.

Kubernetes does not implement this itself. A **CNI plugin** (Calico, Cilium, Flannel and others) wires up each Pod's network interface and routes between nodes. Without a working CNI, Pods stay in `ContainerCreating`.

sections.code:
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,PODCIDR:.spec.podCIDR
kubectl exec web -- ip addr show eth0
sections.title: Inspect Pod IPs and nodes
sections.note: Pod IPs are ephemeral: a replaced Pod gets a new address. That is why Services exist.

sections.title: Cluster DNS with CoreDNS
sections.body:
CoreDNS runs as a Deployment in `kube-system` and is exposed by the `kube-dns` Service. The kubelet writes its address into each Pod's `/etc/resolv.conf`, together with a **search path** so short names work.

A Service `api` in namespace `shop` is resolvable as `api` (same namespace), `api.shop`, or the full name `api.shop.svc.cluster.local`.

head: Resource
Name
Notes
rows: Stable per-Pod name via headless Service

sections.code:
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- sh
# inside the Pod:
cat /etc/resolv.conf
nslookup kubernetes.default
nslookup api.shop.svc.cluster.local
sections.title: Look at resolv.conf and query DNS
sections.note: `ndots:5` means names with fewer than five dots are tried against the search path first.

sections.title: CoreDNS health
sections.body: If name resolution fails cluster-wide, check `kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns` and read the logs with `kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-dns`.

exercises.title: Find Pod IPs
exercises.prompt: List all Pods in every namespace with their IPs and nodes.
exercises.expected: A table with IP and NODE columns for every Pod.

exercises.title: Resolve a Service
exercises.prompt: Run a temporary busybox Pod and resolve the built-in kubernetes Service.
exercises.expected: The name resolves to the ClusterIP of the API server, typically 10.96.0.1.

questions.question: Which statement matches the Kubernetes network model?
options: Pods must use NAT to reach other nodes
Every Pod has its own IP and can reach all Pods without NAT
Pods on different nodes cannot communicate by default
questions.explain: The model requires a flat, NAT-free Pod network.

questions.question: What component actually implements Pod networking?
questions.explain: The CNI plugin configures Pod interfaces and inter-node routing.

questions.question: From namespace shop, which name resolves Service api in namespace billing?
questions.explain: Use <svc>.<namespace>; the search path completes it to the full FQDN.

questions.question: Which Pod runs cluster DNS?
questions.explain: CoreDNS serves the kube-dns Service in kube-system.

lessons.title: Services: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer
lessons.summary: Give a changing set of Pods one stable address, and expose it inside or outside the cluster.
objectives: Write a Service that selects Pods by label
Choose between ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer and headless
Diagnose a Service with no endpoints

sections.title: A stable front for ephemeral Pods
sections.body:
A **Service** gives a set of Pods a stable virtual IP and DNS name. Membership is defined by a **label selector**; the control plane keeps an EndpointSlice with the ready Pod IPs, and `kube-proxy` on each node programs rules that load-balance traffic to them.

`port` is what clients connect to, `targetPort` is the container port, and `nodePort` (when used) is the port opened on every node.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
sections.title: A ClusterIP Service
sections.note: ClusterIP is the default type and is reachable only inside the cluster.

sections.title: Service types
head: Type
Reachable from
Use for
rows: Production external traffic on cloud providers

sections.code:
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80 --target-port=8080
kubectl get svc web
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web
kubectl describe svc web
sections.title: Create and inspect
sections.note: If Endpoints is empty, the selector matches no ready Pods.

sections.title: Selector mismatches and readiness
sections.body: A Service with no endpoints is almost always a label typo or Pods failing their readiness probe. Pods that are not Ready are removed from the Service by design.

sections.code:
kubectl patch svc web -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
kubectl get svc web
# headless: set clusterIP: None in the manifest, then
kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- nslookup web-headless
sections.title: NodePort and headless variants
sections.note: A headless Service returns one A record per ready Pod instead of a single virtual IP.

exercises.title: Expose a Deployment
exercises.prompt: Create a Deployment of nginx and expose it as a ClusterIP Service on port 80.
exercises.command: kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 && kubectl expose deployment web --port=80
exercises.solution: kubectl get svc web shows a CLUSTER-IP.

exercises.title: Check endpoints
exercises.prompt: Show the Pod IPs backing the web Service.
exercises.expected: One IP:80 entry per ready web Pod.
exercises.hint: If empty, compare kubectl get svc web -o wide selector with Pod labels.

questions.question: What does a Service use to choose its Pods?
Which Service type opens a port on every node?
questions.explain: NodePort opens a port in 30000-32767 on each node.

questions.question: A Service has no endpoints. Likely cause?
questions.explain: Empty endpoints mean no Ready Pod matches the selector.

questions.question: What does clusterIP: None create?
options: A headless Service returning Pod IPs
questions.explain: Headless Services skip the virtual IP and expose Pod IPs through DNS.

modules.title: Ingress and traffic control
modules.summary: External routing, TLS, policies and debugging.

lessons.title: Ingress and ingress controllers
lessons.summary: Route HTTP and HTTPS traffic by host and path through one entry point.
objectives: Explain why an Ingress needs a controller
Write host and path routing rules

sections.title: Layer 7 routing
sections.body:
A **Service** of type LoadBalancer costs one cloud load balancer per Service. An **Ingress** instead describes HTTP routing rules, and an **ingress controller** (ingress-nginx, Traefik, HAProxy and others) watches those objects and configures a shared proxy.

An Ingress object does nothing on its own. If no controller is installed, requests are never routed. Select the controller with `ingressClassName`.

sections.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: shop
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts: [shop.example.com]
      secretName: shop-tls
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api
                port:
                  number: 80
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web
                port:
                  number: 80
sections.title: Host, path and TLS routing
sections.note: `pathType: Prefix` matches `/api` and `/api/users`; `Exact` matches only the identical path.

sections.code:
kubectl create secret tls shop-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key
kubectl get ingressclass
kubectl get ingress shop
kubectl describe ingress shop
curl -H 'Host: shop.example.com' http://<controller-ip>/api
sections.title: Create the TLS Secret and verify
sections.note: The Secret must be in the same namespace as the Ingress.

items.title: Confirm the controller
items.body: `kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx` and `kubectl get ingressclass`.

items.title: Check the backend Service
items.body: `kubectl get endpoints api` must list Pod IPs.

items.title: Match host and path
items.body: The Host header must match a rule, and the pathType must cover the path.

sections.title: Gateway API
sections.body: The Gateway API is the more expressive successor to Ingress, with roles for infrastructure and application teams. Ingress remains widely used and stable.

exercises.title: List classes and Ingresses
exercises.prompt: Show available ingress classes and all Ingresses in the cluster.
exercises.command: kubectl get ingressclass && kubectl get ingress -A
exercises.expected: The installed controllers' classes and each Ingress with its ADDRESS.

exercises.title: Create a TLS Secret
exercises.prompt: Create a TLS Secret named shop-tls from tls.crt and tls.key.
exercises.hint: Generate a test pair with openssl req -x509 -nodes -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt -subj /CN=shop.example.com

questions.question: What happens if you create an Ingress with no controller installed?
questions.explain: The Ingress is only configuration; a controller must act on it.

questions.question: Where does TLS get its certificate in an Ingress?
questions.explain: tls.secretName references a TLS Secret in the same namespace.

questions.question: Which pathType matches /api/users for path /api?
questions.explain: Prefix matches on path segments, so /api/users matches /api.

lessons.title: NetworkPolicies and debugging connectivity
lessons.summary: Restrict Pod traffic with default-deny and explicit allow rules, then debug when traffic fails.
objectives: Write allow rules with pod and namespace selectors

sections.title: Open by default, closed by policy
sections.body:
By default all Pods accept traffic from anywhere. A **NetworkPolicy** selects Pods and, once any policy selects a Pod for a direction, only traffic **explicitly allowed** is permitted for that direction. Policies are additive; there are no deny rules.

Policies are enforced by the CNI plugin. Calico and Cilium enforce them; plain Flannel does not, and the objects are silently ignored.

sections.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
sections.title: Default deny all ingress in a namespace
sections.note: `podSelector: {}` selects every Pod in the namespace. Add `Egress` to policyTypes to also block outbound traffic, and remember to allow DNS if you do.

sections.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-web-to-api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: web
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
sections.title: Allow web and monitoring to reach the API
sections.note: Entries under `from` are OR'd. Putting `podSelector` and `namespaceSelector` in the same entry would AND them.

sections.title: Egress and DNS
sections.body: When you default-deny egress, Pods can no longer resolve names. Add an egress rule allowing UDP and TCP port 53 to the kube-dns Pods in kube-system.

items.title: Is the Pod Ready?
items.body: `kubectl get pods -o wide` and `kubectl describe pod`.

items.title: Does DNS resolve?
items.body: `kubectl exec` into a Pod and run `nslookup <svc>`.

items.title: Hit the Pod IP directly
items.body: `curl http://<podIP>:<port>` bypasses the Service to isolate the layer.

sections.code:
kubectl run netshoot --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never -- bash
kubectl debug -it pod/api-0 --image=busybox:1.36 --target=api
sections.title: Throwaway debug tools
sections.note: `kubectl debug` attaches an ephemeral container for images that lack shell tools.

exercises.title: Default deny
exercises.prompt: Apply a default-deny ingress policy to namespace shop and list policies.
exercises.command: kubectl apply -f default-deny.yaml && kubectl get networkpolicy -n shop

exercises.title: Test blocked traffic
exercises.prompt: From a Pod without the allowed label, try to reach the api Service with a short timeout.
exercises.command: kubectl run probe -n shop --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- wget -qO- -T 3 http://api
exercises.hint: A timeout, not a refusal, indicates a policy drop.

questions.question: What is the effect of a policy with podSelector {} and no ingress rules?
options: Denies all ingress to every Pod in the namespace
questions.explain: An empty selector matches all Pods; with no allow rules nothing is permitted.

questions.question: Can you write an explicit deny rule?
options: No, policies are allow-only and additive
questions.explain: Standard NetworkPolicies only allow; denial comes from selection without a matching allow.

questions.question: A policy has a podSelector and a namespaceSelector as separate list items under from. How are they combined?
questions.explain: Separate list items are OR'd; in one item they are AND'd.

questions.question: Policies have no effect on your cluster. Likely cause?
options: CNI plugin does not enforce NetworkPolicy
